content.comment_body: Hello! I'm new here and seeking assistance. I've searched online but haven't found a solution to my problem. I'm using a [product_name] with an [product_name] expansion and have connected a three-wire PT100 sensor according to diagrams from [company_name] and the probe manufacturer. My program is simple; I just want to display the temperature on an [product_name] display for now. I'm using an analog amplifier set to PT100/PT1000 with 0.1 resolution and have configured the message text to show one decimal place. Everything seems to be functioning, but when testing, I notice the temperature jumps in 0.3 degree increments and doesn't show the values in between. Am I missing something? Thanks in advance for any help!

The issue is caused by the limited 10-bit resolution of the analog inputs in [product_name]. The A/D converter turns any input (whether voltage, current, or PT100/1000) into 0–1000 units. The [product_name] expansion sets a temperature range from -50 to 200 °C, so the resolution becomes 0.25°C per unit (250/1000 = 0.25). As [product_name]'s system uses integer values only (not float or real values), decimal places aren't truly processed—it's just for display formatting. Selecting 0.1 resolution for PT100/PT1000 only alters how many decimal places are shown in the message text, not the actual measurable resolution. For resolution 1 with no decimal place selected, the text will show values from -50 to 200 °C, updating by 4 units per 1°C, and the system rounds the value. For 0.1 resolution with one decimal displayed, the text shows -50.0 to 200.0 °C, updating by 1 unit per 0.25°C, but again rounding occurs. Examples: At 0.1 resolution, readings go like 0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.3, showing jumps of 0.2°C or 0.3°C when the unit changes.
It's helpful to use the simulation feature to better understand how this operates.
A suggestion: The "Average value" block in [product_name] may make the displayed temperature appear smoother, though it doesn't improve measurement precision.
Thank you! Your explanation really clarified my issue. I need to see 0.1°C resolution for my application, so I might need a stand-alone temperature controller.
This only works well if your measurement range is exactly 100 °C. For instance: -50 to 50°C, -30 to 70°C, -20 to 80°C, or 0 to 100°C.

analysis.insight_summary: Users discovered that the displayed temperature resolution using [product_name] with the [product_name] expansion is restricted by the analog-to-digital conversion and the way integer values are processed internally. The system can't truly display 0.1°C increments because of its 10-bit input and fixed measurement range, resulting in visible steps of around 0.2–0.3°C. Adjusting display settings only formats the output; it doesn't actually increase measurement granularity.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect to see temperature changes smoothly in 0.1°C steps on the device's screen, allowing for precise and accurate monitoring of small variations.
